paras: The attempted lynching of Thomas Olson was a mob threat against a 17-year-old Swedish laborer held in the jail at Aurora, Illinois, on October 2, 1881, after he was accused of fatally stabbing Otto Freese the night before. Officials removed Olson secretly while a crowd gathered, and a party of about 100 young men that set out on October 4 to lynch him turned back before reaching Geneva. The Chicago Tribune covered the case beside its report of a lynching at Bloomington, and a short wire item ran across the upper Midwest.

Olson, his brother Ole and Louis Wester were described as young Swedes employed at the tile works east of Aurora who had spent the evening of October 1 drinking in saloons downtown. Freese, about 20 or just 21, was the only son of Daniel Freese, a saloonkeeper, and the papers described his family as respectable Germans.

Shortly before midnight, Freese and a group of serenaders met the Olsons on Main street in front of the Congregational Church, and after remarks about their singing Freese was stabbed in the neck and bled to death. Ole Olson and Wester were arrested at the scene, and Thomas Olson was found at his boarding-house the next morning and placed in the city lock-up.

Crowds gathered on Sunday morning on the island where the jail stood; the Tribune's correspondent wrote that lynch law "was publicly advocated" and that the lynchers had ropes ready and an hour fixed. Mayor Phillips and the city attorney had the prisoner hurried from the jail into a waiting carriage for the county jail at Geneva before the crowd knew what had happened. The wire report said simply that the jail was surrounded all forenoon and the prisoner "had to be taken to Geneva to avoid lynching."

At about 1 a.m. on October 4, a party of about 100 young men, chiefly railroaders and friends of Freese, started for Geneva with the declared purpose of lynching Olson. According to the Tribune's Aurora dispatch, they pressed on through rain with the help of liquor until the leader's horse fell, then turned back. An Elgin dispatch reported that officers sent by Sheriff Carlisle had already brought Olson secretly to the Elgin city jail on Sunday night, as a "vigilance committee" gathered at Aurora.

Interviewed at Elgin, Olson said he had been drunk and that someone shoved him; by October 3 he had confessed the stabbing while denying any intent to kill. In mid-October Ole Olson swore that the brothers had bought their liquor at Daniel Freese's saloon, and four saloonkeepers were indicted for illegal practices. Defense counsel and private prosecutors were retained, but no report of Olson's trial, or of action against members of the crowd, appears in the coverage.

The Tribune ran its Aurora dispatch on the front page of October 3 under a deck calling the stabbing "Another Horrible and Unprovoked Murder," on the same page as its Bloomington lynching report and a reader's letter denouncing mob violence. Two days later it mocked the night party as "bloodthirsty as a band of Missouri outlaws," while its Elgin correspondent pictured Olson as a "harmless-looking" boy who wept as he told his story.

A brief Chicago wire item appeared on October 3 in the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Rock Island Argus, the Argus printing it above a Bloomington lynching dispatch. A crime-column version ending with the prisoner sent to Geneva "to avert a lynching" ran the next week in Wisconsin and Dakota weeklies. Later notices turned to the sale of liquor to minors. No report names anyone's race; the accused was called a Swede, once a Norwegian, and the victim the son of a German family.

Olson's age was given as 17 in the wire reports and the Tribune but as "only about 15" in the Ottawa Free Trader. Reports also differed on where he was held: the wire said Geneva, the Tribune's Elgin correspondent, who interviewed him, placed him at Elgin, and its Aurora dispatch said Sycamore.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd gathered at the Aurora jail with lynching openly advocated and ropes ready, and a party of about 100 later set out to lynch the prisoner, who was never reached (A2, A6).

No one was killed by the crowd: Thomas Olson was removed from the jail before the crowd acted and the party of about 100 turned back before reaching Geneva (A2, A6). It was an attempted lynching of a man described as a Swede, accused of murder (A3, A6).

The Chicago wire brief (A3, A4), the Tribune's own Aurora correspondent (A2, A7) and the Ottawa Free Trader's Aurora account (A12) agree on the stabbing, the arrest and, in A2-A4, the crowd at the jail and the removal to avoid lynching.

framing.detail: Chicago Tribune headlined the stabbing 'Another Horrible and Unprovoked Murder' beside its Bloomington lynching coverage and a letter against mob violence, later ridiculed the lynching party and portrayed Olson as a weeping 'harmless-looking' boy.
Midwestern dailies and weeklies ran a short wire or crime-column item ending with the removal to Geneva 'to avoid lynching' or 'to avert a lynching'.
Later items turned to liquor sold to minors, noting the drink came from the victim's father's saloon.
